    Katherine Frields
    UCI Data Science B.S & Earth System Science B.S | Columbia LEAP REU Student

    The universe is a machine and every scientific discipline, from physics to chemistry to the depths of math itself, offers us a glimpse into its near infinite complexity. Moreover, between each of these fields lie endless myraids of interactions, and in no other field is this more true that Climate Data Science.

    Through the convergence of machine learning and climate science I aim to push forward our understanding of our planet and our future. With the the growing effects of climate change on human populations, accurate and applicable climate projections are more relevant than ever before. And with near yearly ground-breaking advancements in AI, and the ever climbing accuracy of AI Climate models, vast opportunities have opened up for rapid advancement in climate projections and scientific knowledge.

    By blending physics with machine learning these models have achieved stable long-term projections at a fraction of the comptuational cost, opening up the door to finer-scale resolving of atmospheric and ocean dynamics. Within the training of these models, lies further potential for improved uncertainty quantification as well as the use of stochastic parameterisation to improve model accuracy.

    My own work in machine learning applications to climate and earth science hhas spanned from microphysics to the globe dynamics. Over my time as a Data Science and Earth Science major at UCI, I have had the opportunity to work on uncertainty quantification for hybrid physics-ML climate models in the ClimSim Online frame. My research demonstrated the potential for confidence loss as an accurate and low-cost method of uncertainty quantifiaction. Moreover, this past summer I had the opportunity to conduct research as part of LEAP, an NSF science and technology center dedicated to Learning the Earth with Artificial Intelligence and Physics. There I worked on developing a diffusion model for the generation of thermodynamic back-trajectories for ice crystal images taken from cirrus clouds.

    I am honored to be a part of the global scientific effort and I am excited to continue my research in this growing field.
